sections.heading: Holy Martyrs Lawrence the Archdeacon, Sixtus Pope of Rome, and Hippolytus

pairs.en: On the same day, the tenth of the month, we remember the holy martyrs LAWRENCE the Archdeacon, SIXTUS Pope of Rome, and HIPPOLYTUS.

*Lawrence — a sea-bass of Christ, I call him —* *roasted through on a bed of coals.* *Wanting an athlete's end and an athlete's glory,* *you ran the race of the sword, Sixtus.* *I see Hippolytus bound to horses,* *playing out a passion that runs against his name.* *On the tenth they roasted Lawrence like a fish.*

These saints lived in the reign of the emperor Decius, in the year 250. Saint Sixtus was from Athens, where he had been taught the lessons of philosophy; and when he came to Rome he was ordained bishop, after Saint Stephen the Pope of Rome had been martyred. Because the persecution of the Christians was then about to break, Saint Sixtus ordered his archdeacon, Saint Lawrence, to put the vessels of the Church of Rome in order; and the godly Lawrence distributed them among the poor.

When Decius returned from Persia, Saint Sixtus was brought before him; and because he would not be persuaded to deny Christ, but openly confessed him true God and maker of all things, he was beheaded, and the man of blessed memory received the crown of martyrdom. Then the archdeacon Lawrence was brought before him as well, and Decius demanded of him, as a debt, the vessels and the money of the Church. So the saint asked for carts, and when he had them he loaded on them the poor and the lame and those wretched people to whom he had given the money, and he brought them to the emperor. When the emperor saw them he flew into a rage, and ordered the saint to be beaten hard and then thrown into prison. And while the saint was there he healed all the sick who came to him. When the tribune Kallinikos, who was in charge of the prison, saw these healings, he believed in Christ and was baptised.

After that Saint Lawrence was set before the emperor again, and because he would not sacrifice to the idols they stretched him out on a red-hot gridiron, with a fire burning underneath it. And the saint, stretched out on it, gave thanks to God and gave up his spirit, receiving the unfading crown of the contest. His holy remains were given a proper burial by Saint Hippolytus. When the ungodly emperor learned of this he sent and had Hippolytus brought, and ordered him beaten with iron *kinaras* — a thin chain set with sharp teeth, also called a “scorpion” — and then tied to wild horses; and dragged by force over a long stretch of ground, the athlete of Christ gave his blessed soul into the hands of God.

Their gathering and feast is kept at a place called the Triconch, near the Capitol of Rome. It is said that seven days after the martyrdom of Saint Hippolytus the emperor Decius and Valerian went on horseback to the theatre, and there they cast away their foul souls. And Decius cried out in the hour of his death and said, “O Hippolytus, like a captive you drag me bound!” And Valerian too cried out, “Hippolytus has bound me with fiery *catenae* and is dragging me” — for in Latin a chain is called a *catena*. These words became known through all Rome, and through Rome the whole inhabited world learned them; and so everyone was strengthened in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ. (Note that the Greek account of these martyrs' contest survives in the Great Lavra, in the monastery of the Iberians, and in others; it begins: “When once a storm of idolatry was sweeping the inhabited world.”)
Saint HERON the Philosopher died in peace.
*Dying a sophist, he was crowned as to the head —* *and by giving his head he crushed the sophist's error.*
The holy SIX martyrs of Bizye finished their course — some with their bones crushed, others with their flesh scraped away.
*Broken bones, and the rending of flesh —* *that is the snatching of crowns from the contest.*
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
This Saint Stephen is commemorated on the third of the present month of August.
Note that my own unworthiness completed the service for this Saint Lawrence, and added a second canon as well.

In the Slavonic Synaxarion the *kinara* is explained as a “scorpion.” A scorpion in turn is an instrument of punishment: a thin, short chain set with very sharp teeth. That is what they beat the saint with.
By “Valerian” he may mean the son of Decius — because the emperor Valerian came to the throne three years later, after Decius was dead.

It may be that this is the philosopher Heron to whom Gregory the Theologian wrote a whole oration when he returned from exile; it begins: “I shall praise the philosopher, even if I am worn out in body — for he is a philosopher; and I shall praise him with very good reason, for he is a philosopher, and I am only a servant of wisdom.”
In the Synaxarion of the Monastery of Dionysios these six are written “those in Libya.”
